request.system:
You are the CULTURE RESEARCHER of a trip-planning team. Find the sights worth visiting at the
destination, matched to the travellers' interests, each with a short history, opening hours and ticket price.

TRIP BRIEF (from the session): {'origin': 'Helsinki', 'destination': 'Lisbon', 'start_date': '2027-05-10', 'end_date': '2027-05-14', 'travellers': 2, 'budget_tier': 'mid', 'total_budget_eur': 2500.0, 'interests': ['history', 'street food'], 'origin_lat': 60.16952, 'origin_lon': 24.93545, 'destination_lat': 38.72509, 'destination_lon': -9.1498, 'destination_country': 'Portugal', 'nights': 4, 'days': 5}
Dates are ISO (YYYY-MM-DD). "travellers" is the number of adults. "nights" = end_date - start_date.

STEPS
1. find_sights(lat, lon, interests) with destination_lat/destination_lon and interests from the brief
   (radius_km 3, limit 15). If the brief has no coordinates, call geocode_place(destination) first.
2. wikivoyage_section(page=<destination city>, section="See"). Its listings have coordinates, hours and prices.
   If the city page has few listings but returns district_pages, read the "See" section of the 1-2 most
   central districts (e.g. "Lisbon/Baixa").
3. Choose 8-12 sights: fit the interests, spread over the city, merge duplicates found by several tools, and
   include at least 3 indoor sights (museums, churches, palaces) for rainy days. No restaurants, cafés or
   food markets: the food researcher covers those.
4. find_sight_hours(destination_lat, destination_lon, radius_km 6) once: OpenStreetMap opening hours and
   entry fees (ticket_eur 0 = free). Match its results to your sights by name (names may be in the local
   language, e.g. "Mosteiro dos Jerónimos" = "Jerónimos Monastery") and fill in hours / ticket_eur, adding its
   source URLs. It also lists museums you may have missed.
5. For the 4-6 most important sights whose summary lacks history, call wiki_summary("<sight name>, <city>")
   and use 2-3 sentences of its extract.
6. Only if hours or tickets are STILL missing for the top sights, call web_search AT MOST TWICE in total, each
   time for several sights at once, e.g. "<sight A> <sight B> <sight C> opening hours ticket price".
FALLBACK: if find_sights fails, build the list from Wikivoyage "See" (and its district pages) and
find_sight_hours.
If Wikivoyage fails too, use web_search "top sights in <city> history opening hours".

TOOL USE: call tools one at a time and keep it short: at most 13 tool calls in total.
Do not repeat a call with the same arguments.

GROUNDING RULES (strict):
- Every place, price, time and link you report must come from a tool result in this conversation.
  Never invent names, prices, opening hours or URLs, and never fill gaps from memory.
- Keep each item's url / source_urls exactly as the tool returned them.
- Keep price_source as the tool gave it: "live" (booking/search sites) or "web_estimate" (read from a web page via web_search).
  A price you read from a web_search result is always "web_estimate".
- If a tool returns {"status": "error"}, read its "reason", then use the fallback described below.
  Mention every failed source in "notes".
- If no tool gives you something, leave it out (or null) and say so in "notes".

OUTPUT: when you are done, reply with ONLY one JSON object inside a ```json fence, nothing before or after it.
Shape: {"results": [Place, ...], "notes": "..."}
Place = {"kind": "sight", "name": str, "lat": number|null, "lon": number|null,
         "summary": str (2-3 sentences: what it is + short history), "budget_tier": null,
         "hours": str|null, "ticket_eur": number|null (0 if free, null if unknown),
         "indoor": true|false|null, "source_urls": [str, ...] (every page the facts came from)}
Example (values are illustrative only):
```json
{"results": [{"kind": "sight", "name": "Belém Tower", "lat": 38.6916, "lon": -9.216,
  "summary": "16th-century fortified tower at the mouth of the Tagus, built to defend Lisbon. A UNESCO World Heritage Site and a symbol of the Age of Discoveries.",
  "budget_tier": null, "hours": "Tu-Su 10:00-17:30", "ticket_eur": 10.0, "indoor": false,
  "source_urls": ["https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Lisbon/Bel%C3%A9m", "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower"]}],
 "notes": "OpenTripMap and Wikivoyage worked; hours for 2 sights unknown."}
```
Use double quotes, no comments, no trailing commas. "notes" is one short paragraph: which sources worked or failed,
fallbacks used, caveats (e.g. estimated prices). Write it in English.

You are an agent. Your internal name is "culture_agent". The description about you is "Finds sights with short histories, opening hours and ticket prices.".

results.name: Aos Restauradores de 1640
results.summary: The Monument to the Restorers (Portuguese: Monumento aos Restauradores) is a monument located in Restauradores Square in Lisbon, Portugal. The monument memorializes the victory of the Portuguese Restoration War. The war, which saw the end of the House of Habsburg and the rise of the House of Braganza, lasted from 1640 to 1668. The monument was designed by António Tomás da Fonseca and erected in 1886.

See:
Lisbon is a city on the water—the River Tagus (Rio Tejo)—built on seven hills that are traversed by trams. This has led to comparisons with San Francisco. To provide access from the southern suburbs, Lisbon has two spectacular bridges. The 25th of April Bridge (Ponte 25 de Abril) combines the design of the San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge with the color of the Golden Gate Bridge, and it's often mistaken for the latter. The Vasco da Gama Bridge (Ponte Vasco da Gama), Europe's longest, was built in the 1990s for Expo '98. One of Lisbon's great landmarks, Cristo Rei, a 28 m statue of Christ the King on an 82 m pedestal, isn't even in Lisbon itself, but across the river in Almada, big enough to be easily seen from the capital.

Alfama:
Built on the hills east of the Baixa, Alfama survived the Great 1755 Earthquake largely intact. Climbing the narrow ancient lanes provides an excellent workout. You can spare your legs by taking the little historic yellow trams that serve the neighborhood. Major sights include Lisbon Cathedral and St. George's Castle.

Bairro Alto:
The Bairro Alto, or "Upper District" (dare we say "High Neighbourhood"), has become Lisbon's youthful, trendy quarter. The district includes the Chiado neighbourhood, known for its numerous historic landmarks and theatres. Among the district's many sights are the São Bento Palace (where the Portuguese parliament meets), the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (a museum of antique art), and the Lisbon Botanical Gardens.

results.name: Ajuda Botanical Gardens
results.summary: The botanical garden of Ajuda is one of the oldest gardens in Europe and is considered the first in Portugal. After the earthquake that occurred in 1755, the homeless Portuguese royal family decided to build a new royal residence at Ajuda but also gardens around it. This 10-acre garden was laid out in from 1858-1873.

results.summary: Good viewpoint in Alfama uphill from the cathedral along tram route. Lovely view over rooftops and river.

results.name: Miradouro da Senhora do Monte
results.summary: The highest viewpoint in Lisbon, at the top of the Graça hill, spread out in front of the small Capela de Nossa Senhora do Monte (founded in 1147, remodelled in the 20th century). To the south you look down over the Castelo de São Jorge, the Mouraria and the Baixa to the Tagus estuary; to the west, from Bairro Alto out to the Monsanto forest; to the north, down the Avenida Almirante Reis valley. It sits a little further out than the viewpoints at Santa Luzia and Portas do Sol, so it is usually quieter, and it is a fine place to watch the sunset.

results.name: Castelo de São Jorge
results.summary: Humans settled on this hill as early as the 8th century BCE, and the first fortifications date from the 1st century BCE. Before the Portuguese conquest in the 1147 Siege of Lisbon, the site was successively occupied by the Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans, and Moors. Sights within the castle include the permanent exhibition of archaeological artefacts with an emphasis on the 11th- and 12th-century Moors, ruins of the former Royal Palace of Alcáçova, a garden with native forest species, and a camera obscura showing the city's sights. results.summary: This is one of the most striking buildings in Lisbon. Its tall dome and white facade makes it a real landmark in Alfama/Eastern Lisbon. Excellent views from the rooftop terrace. Construction began in 1681, then halted until the dome was added in 1966 and then converted to the National Pantheon. Amália Rodrigues, queen of fado, is buried here, and fresh roses can be seen on the tomb. The church also has wide viewing platform on the rooftop all around its dome. results.title: Jerónimos Monastery
results.description: Building in Santa Maria de Belém, Lisbon District, Portugal
results.extract:
The Jerónimos Monastery or Hieronymites Monastery (Portuguese: Mosteiro dos Jerónimos, pronounced [muʃˈtɐjɾu ðu(ʒ) ʒɨˈɾɔnimuʃ]) is a former monastery of the Order of Saint Jerome near the Tagus river in the parish of Belém, in the Lisbon Municipality, Portugal. It became the necropolis of the Portuguese royal dynasty of Aviz in the 16th century but was secularized on 28 December 1833 by state decree and its ownership transferred to the charitable institution, Real Casa Pia de Lisboa.
The Jerónimos Monastery is one of the most prominent examples of the late Portuguese Gothic Manueline style of architecture in Lisbon. It was erected in the early 1500s near the launch point of Vasco da Gama's first journey, and its construction funded by a tax on the profits of the yearly Portuguese India Armadas. In 1880, da Gama's remains and those of the poet Luís de Camões (who celebrated da Gama's first voyage in his 1572 epic poem The Lusiad), were moved to new carved tombs in the nave of the monastery's church, only a few meters away from the tombs of the kings Manuel I and John III, whom da Gama had served.

results.title: Belém Tower
results.extract:
Belém Tower (Portuguese: Torre de Belém, pronounced [ˈtoʁɨ ðɨ βɨˈlɐ̃j]; literally: Bethlehem Tower), officially the Tower of Saint Vincent (Portuguese: Torre de São Vicente), is a 16th-century fortification located in Lisbon, Portugal, which served as a point of embarkation and disembarkation for Portuguese explorers and as a ceremonial gateway to Lisbon. The tower symbolizes Portugal's maritime and colonial power in early modern Europe. It was built during the height of the Portuguese Renaissance and is a prominent example of the Portuguese Manueline style, but it also incorporates other architectural styles, such as the minarets, which are inspired by Moorish architecture. The structure was built from lioz limestone, a material local to the Lisbon region, and is composed of a bastion and a 30-metre (100 ft) four-storey tower.
Since 1983, the tower has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site, along with the Jerónimos Monastery. It is often portrayed as a symbol of Europe's Age of Discoveries and as a metonym for Portugal or Lisbon, given its landmark status.
